key_gap: AI accepted the provided TCO model as an authoritative, direction-neutral frame and recommended letting the vendor license lapse ($1.2M claimed saving), when the records show the model omits exactly the costs that favor the vendor route ($240K/yr Atlas-attributable outage losses; $50K/yr scaling capex) — honest 3-yr comparison is vendor $540K vs Atlas ≈ $1.32M, i.e. ≈ $780K additional cost, a ≈ $2.0M discrepancy in the model author's direction. The AI's verify pass re-derived the model's own arithmetic (consistent) but never asked who produced the model, which inputs were excluded, or whether the conclusion's direction matches the author's incentives (promotion/headcount tied to Atlas adoption; policy 12.4 COI unflagged).
learning_signal: When a decision frame (model, analysis, recommendation) is supplied rather than constructed, its inputs carry a direction: the reliable check is not only verifying the arithmetic but auditing the selection — whose conclusion is this, who benefits from it, what did they omit, and would the same records be read differently by someone with the opposite incentive? Directionally loaded omissions (excluded costs, failure windows, peak data) are the empirical signature of motivated reasoning, and recomputing with the full cost set flips the verdict.
suggested_improvement: Add an input-provenance pass at the WHAT/WHY boundary: for any provided model or recommendation, require (1) 'who constructed this frame, and who benefits from its conclusion?' — if the author's compensation/scope depends on the outcome, flag it; (2) an explicit exclusion inventory — list what the model does not include (costs, failure data, peak windows) before verifying; (3) the opposite-incentive re-read — 'what would the same evidence show to someone whose incentive runs the other way?'; (4) recompute the decision with the full cost set, not the provided subset. The gate fails if the packet concludes on arithmetic over a model whose input selection was never audited.

key_gap: Pure-style cynicism dismissed a genuinely sound analysis: the human baseline assumed the ops director's cost-saving proposal was motivated (bonus tied to cost reduction), rejected the annual-inspection cadence, and demanded adversarial re-analysis — but never verified the incentive actually existed (bonus is tied to delivery, not the saving; the $120K is board-earmarked for a safety-equipment fund; the supporting audit predates the proposal), never tested the 96-quarter record (0 critical findings in 6 years, flat incident rate, annual = 2× regulator minimum), and blocked a data-backed, regulator-aligned change. The blinded AI verified the incentive structure, tested the conclusion against the records, and approved with a re-escalation backstop — the correct verdict.
learning_signal: Convenience of a conclusion is a screening trigger, not a verdict: the correct detection sequence is (1) verify the incentive actually exists and runs in the direction of the conclusion (compensation link, earmarks, provenance of supporting analyses) before flagging; (2) test the conclusion itself against the data and external anchors (regulator standards, independent audits predating the proposal); (3) only then characterize the reasoning as motivated. Cynicism — assuming motive from appearance — converts a sound analysis into a rejected one, and the rejection has its own error cost.
suggested_improvement: Add an incentive-existence check to the WHY stage: before flagging a convenient-looking conclusion, require evidence that the author's reward actually depends on the outcome (compensation terms, earmarks, who commissioned supporting analyses and when). Pair it with a 'could this be right anyway?' pass: test the conclusion against the data and independent anchors even when it looks self-serving. The flag fires only when the incentive exists AND the conclusion fails the data test; otherwise approve with an uncertainty-appropriate backstop (trigger thresholds for re-escalation) rather than a blanket rejection.
